works.title: Workday
works.summary: Create intuitive and visually stunning user experiences that engage and convert.
works.challenge: Workday's mobile experience had grown feature by feature until the core task — checking and approving requests — took four taps and two screens nobody could name.
works.solution: We rebuilt the app around the three things people actually opened it for, moved everything else behind an explicit browse mode, and shipped a component library so new features stop accreting on the home screen.

quote.text: They removed more than they added, and the product got dramatically better for it.
quote.author: Val Kobal

approach.title: Watched people use it
approach.body: Twelve sessions with real approvers. The pattern was immediate: nobody browsed, everyone arrived with one task.

approach.title: Cut the surface
approach.body: We mapped every widget to a job. Twenty-eight had no job, so they moved behind an explicit browse mode.

approach.title: Rebuilt around three tasks
approach.body: Approve, check status, submit. Everything else got out of their way.

approach.title: Shipped a system, not screens
approach.body: A component library with real states, so new features stop landing on the home screen.

works.outcome: Approvals now take two taps from a cold open. The team ships new features into the browse mode instead of the home screen, which is what stops the problem returning.

works.title: Verda Botanics
works.summary: A seasonal campaign system for a skincare brand sending to nine segments.
works.challenge: Nine segments, four seasonal drops a year, and a designer rebuilding every send by hand. Dark mode inverted the brand's pale greens into something closer to grey sludge.
works.solution: A seasonal module set with explicit dark-mode variants, so the palette survives inversion, plus a swatch system the team swaps per drop without touching markup.

quote.text: Dark mode used to turn our greens to mud. Now the brand looks like the brand in every inbox.
quote.author: Elena Rossi

approach.title: Audited a year of sends
approach.body: Four drops, nine segments, and almost no reuse between them. The work was being redone rather than composed.

approach.title: Designed for inversion first
approach.body: We picked the palette by testing what survives a forced dark-mode conversion, not by picking swatches and hoping.

approach.title: Built swappable seasons
approach.body: One structure, a swatch set per drop. A seasonal refresh is now a colour change, not a rebuild.

approach.title: Handed over properly
approach.body: A short guide and one session with the team who send it.

works.outcome: A campaign that took the best part of a day now takes under an hour, and revenue per send is up 24% on the same list.

works.title: Kestrel Athletics
works.summary: An identity for a running brand that needed to work at 40mph and on a label.
works.challenge: Kestrel's mark was drawn for a website and then stretched onto everything else. On a shoe it turned to mush; on a race bib it disappeared.
works.solution: A mark built from the smallest application up — a bib number at ten metres — then scaled, with a weight set for print, embroidery and screen rather than one file forced everywhere.

quote.text: They started with the hardest place it had to work and everything else fell out of that.
quote.author: George El Nachar

approach.title: Started at the worst case
approach.body: A race bib seen at ten metres, in rain. Anything that survives that survives a website.

approach.title: Drew weights, not sizes
approach.body: Embroidery, screen print, foil and screen each need different stroke weights. One file scaled does not work.

approach.title: Tested on the actual substrates
approach.body: Printed, stitched and photographed before signing anything off.

approach.title: Wrote rules for the suppliers
approach.body: Guidelines aimed at the factory, not at a design team.

works.outcome: One mark that holds from an embroidered chest logo to a stadium banner, and prompted recall up 41% after the first season.

works.title: Hakka's Dine
works.summary: Modern restaurant booking and food delivery platform design.
works.challenge: Bookings and delivery lived on two different platforms with two different logins, and the restaurant was paying commission on both.
works.solution: One site handling both, built on Next.js with the kitchen's own order flow, so Hakka's keeps the margin and the customer keeps one account.

quote.text: We stopped paying two platforms to stand between us and our own customers.
quote.author: Imran Chowdhury

approach.title: Followed the money
approach.body: Two platforms, two commissions, two logins. We costed what each was actually buying them — it was not much.

approach.title: One account, both jobs
approach.body: Booking and delivery share a customer, so they share a login and a history.

approach.title: Built for the kitchen too
approach.body: The order screen was designed with the staff who read it at 8pm on a Friday.

approach.title: Made it fast on purpose
approach.body: A performance budget checked on every pull request, because a slow menu is an abandoned order.

works.outcome: Direct orders are up 64% and the commission line is gone. The kitchen screen has not needed a change since launch.

works.title: Northline Logistics
works.summary: A quiet, durable identity for a freight business that did not want a loud one.
works.challenge: Northline had three logos in active use and materials that looked like a template, which read as small to the enterprise clients they were pitching.
works.solution: A typographic identity with no illustrative mark at all — a custom wordmark, a strict grid, and vehicle livery treated as part of the system.

quote.text: They talked us out of a logo. It was the right call and we would not have got there alone.
quote.author: George El Nachar

approach.title: Asked what was actually wrong
approach.body: The work was respected. The materials looked like a template, and enterprise buyers read that as small.

approach.title: Argued against a logo
approach.body: A mark would have dated. A wordmark and a strict grid would not.

approach.title: Designed for a lorry first
approach.body: If it works at fifty metres on a moving vehicle, it works on a business card.

approach.title: Wrote the rules down
approach.body: Guidelines their print supplier could follow without calling us.

works.outcome: Three identity systems became one. Inbound enquiries rose 29%, and the system has needed no revisions since.

works.title: Medicove Intl
works.challenge: Nearly a third of patients abandoned onboarding, and the drop-off was concentrated among older users and anyone using a screen reader.
works.solution: We shortened the flow to four steps, made every field recoverable, and rebuilt it to WCAG 2.2 AA with real assistive-technology testing rather than an audit checklist.

quote.text: The accessibility work changed the design, and the design got better for everybody.
quote.author: Elena Rossi

approach.title: Tested with the people failing
approach.body: Not a general sample — older patients and screen-reader users, because that is where the drop-off was.

approach.title: Shortened before styling
approach.body: Eleven steps became four. Most of what was removed existed for internal reporting, not for the patient.

approach.title: Made every field recoverable
approach.body: Nothing is lost on a mistake, a timeout or a back button. That alone fixed a third of the abandonment.

approach.title: Verified with real tools
approach.body: NVDA and VoiceOver, not an automated checker signing off on its own work.

works.outcome: Drop-off fell 31% and the flow now conforms to WCAG 2.2 AA. The accessibility patterns became the studio's internal reference.

works.title: Fintech Pro
works.summary: Secure and intuitive financial management dashboard.
works.challenge: Forty widgets on one dashboard, and a support queue full of people asking where to find a single number.
works.solution: A dashboard built around three questions the data actually answers, with everything else moved into a searchable explore mode.

quote.text: Our customers stopped emailing us to ask where things were.
quote.author: Sarah Jenkins

approach.title: Read the support queue
approach.body: Four hundred tickets, sorted. Most asked where one number lived.

approach.title: Answered three questions
approach.body: We built the dashboard around the three the data actually answers, and moved the rest into search.

approach.title: Designed the charts as components
approach.body: One vocabulary for axes, empty states and loading, so nothing reads as a different product.

approach.title: Kept the depth, hid the clutter
approach.body: Nothing was deleted. It stopped competing for the same screen.

works.outcome: Support tickets dropped 41% in a quarter and time to first insight more than halved. Nobody has asked for the old dashboard.

works.title: Parallel Labs
works.summary: A research tool redesigned around the two hours a week people actually spend in it.
works.challenge: Parallel had built for the power user who lives in the tool. Analytics said the median user opened it twice a week for an hour, and spent most of that reorienting.
works.solution: A workspace that remembers where you were, surfaces what changed since, and puts the two recurring tasks one click from the door.

quote.text: We had designed for the person who never leaves. Almost nobody is that person.
quote.author: Sarah Jenkins

approach.title: Read the analytics first
approach.body: The gap between who they designed for and who actually used it was the whole brief.

approach.title: Designed for returning, not arriving
approach.body: Most sessions are a resumption. The interface now treats that as the default case.

approach.title: Made change visible
approach.body: A what-changed-since-you-left view removed most of the reorienting time.

approach.title: Kept the power features
approach.body: Nothing was taken away from the heavy users; it stopped being the first thing everyone else saw.

works.outcome: Time to resume work fell by nearly two thirds, and weekly retention rose 19% without a single new feature.

works.title: Aurora Health
works.summary: A modular email system for a health brand sending to six segments a week.
works.challenge: Every campaign was rebuilt from scratch, and roughly one in five broke in Outlook after it had already gone out.
works.solution: Twelve tested modules the team assembles in Klaviyo, with dark-mode and image-off handling built in, so a campaign takes an hour instead of a day.

quote.text: Campaigns take an hour now, and nothing has broken in Outlook since launch.
quote.author: Sarah Jenkins

approach.title: Audited what broke
approach.body: One in five sends failed in Outlook. Every campaign had been rebuilt from scratch, so every campaign found new ways to break.

approach.title: Built modules, not emails
approach.body: Twelve sections that compose into any campaign, each tested once and reused forever.

approach.title: Handled the awkward cases
approach.body: Dark mode, image blocking and Gmail clipping designed for rather than discovered later.

approach.title: Taught the team
approach.body: A short guide and one session. They have not needed us since.

works.outcome: A campaign now takes an hour instead of a day, click-through is up 38%, and nothing has broken in Outlook since launch.
